blocks.body: Present Perfect: Time Expressions — just, already, yet, ever, never, for, since, recently, lately, so far, and unfinished time periods that connect the past with the present.

{"level":"A1–C2","intro":"Time expressions help show a link between a past action and the present moment, but no marker chooses the tense by itself. Always check the context: a present result, experience up to now, or a period that is still open.","rules":[{"label":"just / already / yet","color":"emerald","text":"Just and already normally go between have/has and V3; yet normally goes at the end of a question or negative.","example":"She has just arrived. / I have already eaten. / He hasn't called yet."},{"label":"ever / never","color":"blue","text":"Ever and never normally go between have/has and V3. Never already has a negative meaning, so it does not take not.","example":"Have you ever been to Spain? / We have never tried it."},{"label":"for / since","color":"amber","text":"For gives a duration; since gives the starting point of a period that reaches the present.","example":"I have lived here for three years. / She has worked here since 2022."},{"label":"recently / lately / so far","color":"violet","text":"Recently and lately refer to a recent period; so far and up to now summarise progress to the present point.","example":"I have recently changed jobs. / We haven't met lately. / So far, we have completed ten tasks."}]}

{"title":"1. Meaning and position","intro":"A marker's normal position matters as much as its meaning.","items":[{"label":"Recent result","title":"have/has + just/already + V3","subtitle":"just = a moment ago; already = before now. Normally: She has just left. / We have already finished."},{"label":"Questions and negatives","title":"yet at the end","subtitle":"Have you finished yet? / I haven't finished yet. Yet is not normally used in an affirmative sentence with this meaning."},{"label":"Experience","title":"have/has + ever/never + V3","subtitle":"Ever is common in experience questions; never appears in an affirmative grammatical form with a negative meaning."},{"label":"Recent period","title":"recently / lately","subtitle":"Recently can go before V3 or at the end; lately most often goes at the end: I haven't seen her lately."},{"label":"Progress up to now","title":"so far / up to now","subtitle":"At the beginning or end: So far, we have finished six tasks. / We have finished six tasks so far."},{"label":"Duration and starting point","title":"for + period / since + point","subtitle":"for two hours, for six months; since Monday, since 2020, since I moved here."}]}

{"title":"2. Context up to the present","sections":[{"label":"Recent result","color":"emerald","description":"Just, already, and yet connect completion or an expected result with now. Already in a question can express surprise.","examples":[{"en":"They have just arrived.","ua":"A very recent action with a result now."},{"en":"Have you already finished?","ua":"The speaker is surprised that it may be complete."}]},{"label":"Experience up to now","color":"blue","description":"Ever asks about experience at any point before now; never says that the experience has not happened. The context must clearly be about experience.","examples":[{"en":"Have you ever been to Rome?","ua":"Experience at any time in your life up to now."},{"en":"I have never travelled alone.","ua":"No such experience up to now."}]},{"label":"Recent period and progress","color":"amber","description":"Recently/lately describe a recent period without a finished date; so far/up to now summarise progress to the present point.","examples":[{"en":"She has worked from home lately.","ua":"A recent period continuing up to now."},{"en":"Up to now, we have solved eight problems.","ua":"A progress total at the present point."}]},{"label":"Unfinished time period","color":"violet","description":"Today, this week, this month, this year can take Present Perfect when the period is still open and the current result matters. Use Past Simple when the period is finished.","examples":[{"en":"I have had two meetings today.","ua":"Today is still in progress; this is the total so far."},{"en":"I had two meetings yesterday.","ua":"Yesterday is a finished period."}]},{"label":"This morning depends on speaking time","color":"rose","description":"This morning does not guarantee Present Perfect: the choice depends on whether the morning is still in progress.","examples":[{"en":"I've answered five emails this morning.","ua":"It is still morning."},{"en":"I answered five emails this morning.","ua":"It is now afternoon or evening."}]}]}

{"title":"3. Present Perfect or Past Simple?","intro":"Present Perfect does not name a finished past time; Past Simple places the action in a completed time period.","rows":[{"en":"I have seen that film. / I saw it last Friday.","ua":"experience up to now / a specific finished time","note":"no finished time / last Friday"},{"en":"I've spoken to Anna today. / I spoke to Anna yesterday.","ua":"today is still open / yesterday is finished","note":"today / yesterday"},{"en":"I've answered five emails this morning. / I answered five emails this morning.","ua":"it is still morning / the morning is over","note":"open / finished period"},{"en":"She has lived here since 2022. / She lived there from 2018 to 2022.","ua":"the situation continues / a finished past period","note":"since / from...to"},{"en":"Have you ever visited Rome? / Did you visit Rome in 2024?","ua":"life experience / a specific year","note":"ever / in 2024"}],"warning":"Yesterday, last..., ...ago, in 2020 point to a finished past time and normally take Past Simple. Today/this week/this morning do not choose the tense automatically: check whether the period is still open. British English commonly uses Present Perfect with just/already/yet; informal American English may use Past Simple: I just ate."}

{"title":"4. Common mistakes","items":[{"label":"Mistake 1","color":"rose","title":"Combining Present Perfect with a finished past time.","wrong":"❌ I have seen him two days ago.","right":"✅ I saw him two days ago."},{"label":"Mistake 2","color":"amber","title":"Mixing up for and since.","wrong":"❌ She has lived here since three years.","right":"✅ She has lived here for three years."},{"label":"Mistake 3","color":"sky","title":"Putting yet before V3 with its normal «still/by now» meaning.","wrong":"❌ I have yet finished the task.","right":"✅ I haven't finished the task yet."},{"label":"Mistake 4","color":"violet","title":"Adding not to never.","wrong":"❌ I haven't never tried it.","right":"✅ I have never tried it."},{"label":"Mistake 5","color":"emerald","title":"Treating today or this morning as an automatic Present Perfect signal.","wrong":"❌ Present Perfect only because the sentence contains today.","right":"✅ First decide whether the time period is still open."}]}

{"title":"5. Short summary","items":["Time expressions are clues, not automatic rules: context decides the tense.","Just, already, ever, never normally go between have/has and V3; yet normally goes at the end of a question or negative.","Use never without not: I have never...","For gives a duration; since gives a starting point.","Recently/lately describe a recent period; so far/up to now summarise progress to now.","Use today, this week, this year, this morning with Present Perfect only when the period is still open or the result matters now.","With yesterday, last..., ...ago, in + a finished year, normally use Past Simple.","The exercises below follow British English: when a completed action with just, already, or yet has a current result, Present Perfect is expected."]}

{"title":"6. Practice","select_title":"Exercise 1. Choose the correct option","select_intro":"Check the context, for / since, and the choice between Present Perfect and Past Simple.","selects":[{"label":"a) I have seen him yesterday. / b) I saw him yesterday.","prompt":"Which option is correct?","answer":"b"},{"label":"a) She has lived here since 2022. / b) She has lived here for 2022.","prompt":"Which option is correct?","answer":"a"}],"options":["a","b"],"input_title":"Exercise 2. Build the sentence","input_intro":"Put the words in the correct order.","inputs":[{"before":"already / has / Leo / finished / the task","after":"→","answer":"Leo has already finished the task."},{"before":"not / we / have / heard / from her / yet","after":"→","accepted":["We have not heard from her yet.","We haven't heard from her yet."]}]}
